title: India Just Opened Its Nuclear Sector to Private Money for the First Time in Sixty Years. The $214 Billion Race Is On.
excerpt: The SHANTI Act lets Adani, Tata, and Jindal build nuclear power plants. IIT Bombay is already training the engineers. And the West is watching closely.
body:
For six decades, India's nuclear energy sector was a state monopoly. No private company could build, own, or operate a nuclear power plant. No foreign investor could put capital into one. The Atomic Energy Act of 1962 drew the line, and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act of 2010 reinforced it — saddling equipment suppliers with open-ended liability that made even foreign technology partnerships unviable.

That era ended in December 2025, when Parliament passed the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India Act — the SHANTI Act — and the president signed it into law.

## What the SHANTI Act Changes

The law repeals both predecessor statutes and replaces them with a single modern framework. Licensed private operators can now build, own, and run nuclear power plants for the first time. Foreign direct investment of up to 49 percent is permitted in certain nuclear activities. A graded liability framework replaces the old flat cap, and the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board finally receives statutory independence.

The numbers behind the opportunity are staggering. India currently has roughly 8.8 GW of installed nuclear capacity. The government's target: 100 GW by 2047. Industry estimates peg the investment required at more than $214 billion.

> **"The United States has signalled interest in "joint innovation and R&D" with India under the new framework."**

## The Private Players Moving In

The corporate response has been swift. Adani has established a full Nuclear Business Group, with a dedicated Vice President for Technology and Engineering and a separate Business Head for Nuclear Energy. Tata Power is positioning its project engineering team for nuclear work. Jindal Steel and Power has assigned a senior advisor specifically for the sector.

At the India Nuclear Business Platform conference in Mumbai, these private entrants sat alongside the old guard — NITI Aayog members, the former chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, and the CEO of NTPC's nuclear arm — in what organisers called "the most consequential nuclear industry gathering in India since the reforms became law."

## The Talent Pipeline

India's premier engineering institutions are responding too. IIT Bombay has launched a dedicated Nuclear Engineering Programme, coordinated through its Green Energy and Sustainability Hub and funded by an alumnus donation. The programme will focus on thorium-based systems — a strategic bet, given that India holds one of the world's largest thorium reserves — and on small modular reactor technology.

The government is developing two reactor types to open the door wider: Bharat Small Reactors, 220 MW pressurised heavy water designs with a proven track record, and Small Modular Reactors for repurposing retiring coal plants and serving remote locations.

## International Interest

The diplomatic community is paying close attention. Nuclear attachés from the British High Commission and the French Embassy attended the Mumbai conference. The United States has signalled interest in "joint innovation and R&D" with India under the new framework. All three countries see India's nuclear pivot as both a commercial opportunity and a strategic alignment — a counterweight to Russia's dominance in nuclear plant exports to the developing world.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora — particularly the significant community of nuclear engineers and energy professionals working at firms like Westinghouse, GE Hitachi, and in the U.S. national labs — the SHANTI Act opens a professional pathway that did not exist before. The 49 percent FDI window means diaspora-led investment vehicles could participate in Indian nuclear projects for the first time.

The road from 8.8 GW to 100 GW will take decades and require capabilities that India's state sector cannot build alone. The SHANTI Act is the legal foundation. Whether it becomes the launchpad depends on how quickly the subordinate regulations are drafted, the AERB is staffed, and the first private projects break ground.
